prompt: Which of these are secrets? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A database connection string with a password in it
choices.why: Right. It grants access.

choices.text: A webhook URL with a token in its query
choices.why: Right. Whoever has the URL can call it.

choices.text: The carrier's public base URL
choices.why: It grants nothing on its own.

choices.text: An administrator's session cookie
choices.why: Right. It lets its holder act as that person.

prompt: Order the three properties of a well-kept secret as the lesson lists them.
items: It is not in the code
It can do only its job
It expires, or is replaced in minutes
trap: Keeping it out of the code comes first; how long it lives comes last.

prompt: The token was committed and the file deleted twenty minutes later. Where is the token now?

choices.text: Nowhere; the delete removed it
choices.why: The delete removed it from the working copy only.

choices.text: In the history and its copies
choices.why: Right. git show printed it from the earlier commit.

choices.text: Only on the developer's laptop
choices.why: Anybody who fetched in those minutes has it too.

choices.text: In the stash
choices.why: Nothing was stashed.

prompt: git log ___ lab-live-token lists every commit that added or removed that string.
A token reached a commit in a private repository and was removed by a force push. How should it be treated?

choices.text: As safe, since the repository is private
choices.why: Private is an audience, not an absence of copies.

choices.text: As safe, since the force push rewrote history
choices.why: Clones and caches made before it still hold it.

choices.text: As leaked: rotate it first
choices.why: Right. Rewriting stops it spreading; it cannot recall copies.

choices.text: As leaked only if somebody reports it
choices.why: Waiting for a report is waiting for the misuse.

prompt: What did -rw-r--r-- on the production config.env mean?

choices.text: Only the owner could read it
choices.why: That is what -rw------- means.

choices.text: Every user could read it
choices.why: Right. chmod 600 removed that.

choices.text: Nobody could write it
choices.why: The owner could.

choices.text: The file was executable
choices.why: There is no x in it.

prompt: Why is a token on a command line worse than one in the environment?

choices.text: Command lines are slower to parse
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

choices.text: Environment variables are encrypted
choices.why: They are not; they are just less visible.

choices.text: ps shows them to every user
choices.why: Right. The environment is readable by the owner and root only.

choices.text: Python refuses tokens in arguments
choices.why: It accepted one in the capture.

prompt: Order these places for a secret, from safest to least safe.
items: Fetched at start-up with a short-lived credential
A file only the program's account can read
trap: Each step down widens who can read it; a command line is readable by everyone.

prompt: Why hand the carrier token to one step through env rather than to the whole workflow?

choices.text: Fewer steps, and less third-party code, hold it
choices.why: Right. A workflow-level secret reaches every step of every job.

choices.text: Because env is the only way GitHub passes secrets
choices.why: It is the narrowest way, not the only one.

choices.text: So the secret appears in the step's name
choices.why: Secrets should appear nowhere.

choices.text: So it is masked; workflow-level secrets are not
choices.why: Masking applies to both.

prompt: On GitLab, what does a protected variable add?

choices.text: It hides the value in job logs
choices.why: That is masked.

choices.text: Only protected refs get it
choices.why: Right. A branch pushed five minutes ago does not get it.

choices.text: It encrypts the value at rest
choices.why: All variables are stored by GitLab; protection is about who receives it.

choices.text: It expires after an hour
choices.why: That describes a federated credential.

prompt: A job declares environment: staging so its secrets come from that environment's ___ .
Why did the base64 line pass through the masker untouched?

choices.text: sed cannot read base64
choices.why: sed read it; there was nothing to replace.

choices.text: The exact bytes of the token were not in it
choices.why: Right. Masking matches the value as registered.

choices.text: The token was rotated before that line
choices.why: Rotation came later.

choices.text: Masking only works on GitHub, not in a shell
choices.why: The lab played the masker on purpose; the limit is the same on GitHub.

prompt: How many lines of production's app.log contained the token?
Which habits keep secrets out of logs, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Log what the program decided, not what it was given
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: No set -x in shared environments
choices.why: Right. It prints expanded variables.

choices.text: grep logs and artifacts for known secrets on purpose
choices.why: Right. A leak search is a test like any other.

choices.text: Encode secrets in base64 before printing them
choices.why: That defeats masking, as the capture showed.

prompt: What does this repository's CI workflow allow its GITHUB_TOKEN to do?

choices.text: Write to the repository
choices.why: Only the release's Publish job may write.

choices.text: Read the code
choices.why: Right. contents: read, and nothing else.

choices.text: Request an OIDC token
choices.why: That is id-token: write, in the deploy job only.

choices.text: Everything the default allows
choices.why: It narrows the default explicitly.

prompt: Match each job of the release workflow to the permission it raises.
A test job and the deploy job run in the same workflow run. Can the test job use id-token: write?

choices.text: Yes, permissions are shared by the workflow
choices.why: They are granted per job when declared per job.

choices.text: No; it is granted per job
choices.why: Right. That is why the release raises them per job.

choices.text: Only if it runs after the deploy
choices.why: Order does not transfer permissions.

choices.text: Yes, if it needs the deploy job
choices.why: needs orders jobs; it shares no permissions.

prompt: What does a pull_request run from a fork receive on GitHub Actions?

choices.text: Every repository secret, like any other run
choices.why: That would hand strangers the secrets.

choices.text: No secrets, and a read-only token
choices.why: Right. It can still check the change.

choices.text: The secrets, masked
choices.why: Masking would not stop a test that sends them elsewhere.

choices.text: Nothing; fork pull requests do not run
choices.why: They run, without secrets.

prompt: A workflow uses pull_request_target and runs the pull request's tests. Why is that dangerous?

choices.text: Because the tests run twice
choices.why: Running twice is not the risk.

choices.text: Because pull_request_target cannot check out code
choices.why: It can, and that is the problem.

choices.text: A stranger's code gets the secrets
choices.why: Right. With that trigger, treat the pull request as data, never as code.

choices.text: Because it skips the required checks
choices.why: Required checks are unaffected.

prompt: Why does the lesson advise keeping jobs that hold secrets small?

choices.text: Small jobs are cheaper per minute
choices.why: Cost is not the reason.

choices.text: Less outside code sits near the secret
choices.why: Right. Every action and package runs with the job's secrets.

choices.text: GitHub limits secrets to jobs under ten steps
choices.why: There is no such limit.

choices.text: So the deploy finishes before the tests
choices.why: Order is set by needs, not size.

prompt: Put the steps of OIDC federation in order.
items: The job asks the CI service for a signed token
The job presents it to the cloud provider
The provider checks the signature and its condition
The provider returns a short-lived credential
trap: The condition is checked before anything is handed back.

prompt: What would happen without attribute_condition in this repository's federation.tf?

choices.text: Nothing; the signature already proves it is this repository
choices.why: The signature proves GitHub issued it, for any repository.

choices.text: Deploys would fail for lack of a key
choices.why: Federation needs no key either way.

choices.text: Any repository on GitHub could obtain credentials
choices.why: Right. The comment calls it the most consequential line.

choices.text: Tokens would last for ever
choices.why: Lifetime is unrelated to the condition.

prompt: What does federation remove from the pipeline?

choices.text: The stored secret
choices.why: Right. Nothing durable exists to leak.

choices.text: The need for least privilege
choices.why: The account still should do only the deploy.

choices.text: The cloud provider's checks
choices.why: The provider checks every exchange.

choices.text: The deploy job
choices.why: The job remains; its key does not.

prompt: The carrier switched to the new token before shipquote did. What did customers see?

choices.text: An error page
choices.why: The fallback answered.

choices.text: The table's price, R$ 21,90
choices.why: Right. The 401 sent price to the fallback, and only the log said so.

choices.text: The carrier's price, R$ 18,60
choices.why: Not until the configuration was updated.

choices.text: A request for the new token
choices.why: Customers never see tokens.

prompt: Order the steps after a secret has leaked.
items: Find and close how it leaked
Clean up the copies you control
trap: Cleaning up first leaves the secret working the whole time.

prompt: How does a provider let a routine rotation happen without an outage?

choices.text: By sending the new token in the old one's place
choices.why: The consumer must still be updated.

choices.text: By accepting two valid secrets for a while
choices.why: Right. Create, deploy, confirm, then revoke.

choices.text: By turning masking off during the change
choices.why: Masking is unrelated.

choices.text: By retrying each request with both tokens
choices.why: That would leak the old one into new requests.

prompt: Match each leak path to the defence the lesson gives.

pairs.left: A config file others can read
A token on a command line

prompt: A team's deploy job uses a cloud key stored as a repository secret, given to the whole workflow, which also runs the test suite. What is the most valuable single change?

choices.text: Mask the key in the logs
choices.why: It is already masked; masking is a net, not a fix.

choices.text: Rotate the key every year
choices.why: Better than never, and it leaves a durable key in reach of every step.

choices.text: Federation, in the deploy job only
choices.why: Right. No stored secret, and only the job that deploys can obtain access.

choices.text: Move the tests to another repository
choices.why: That changes nothing about the key.
